etymologies.etymologyHTML: trivial (comparative more trivial, superlative most trivial)

definitions.definition: Ignorable; of little significance or value.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 16, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: "All which details, I have no doubt, Jones, who reads this book at his Club, will pronounce to be excessively foolish, trivial, twaddling, and ultra-sentimental."

quote.citation: 2019, Li Huang, James Lambert, “Another Arrow for the Quiver: A New Methodology for Multilingual Researchers”, in Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development, →DOI, page 11:
quote.text: In fact, the influence of signage in a certain area may exist anywhere on a continuum from profoundly effective to utterly trivial or completely insignificant, irrespective of the intent motivating the signs.

quote.citation: 1842, Thomas De Quincey, “Cicero”, in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine:
quote.text: As a scholar, meantime, he was trivial, and incapable of labour.

definitions.definition: (taxonomy) Relating to or designating the name of a species; specific as opposed to generic.
(algebra, of an algebraic structure or ideal thereof) Containing only one element; having an underlying set which is a singleton.
(mathematics) Of, relating to, or being the simplest possible case.
(philosophy) Indistinguishable in case of truth or falsity.
(obsolete) Any of the three liberal arts forming the trivium.
